run.question: We're getting mapping errors and slow indexing on our events index. Can you check the field mappings for our app-188-index-* indexes and tell me if any have an unusually high number of fields? What's the exact field count for each?

report.summary: Mappings for the four indices matching app-188-index-* were read from the registered Elasticsearch target (state at 2026-11-22T10:23:58–10:24:13Z, target m0-otel-20260909). Three of them — app-188-index-a, app-188-index-b and app-188-index-c — each have exactly 10 top-level mapped fields with identical names (@timestamp, action, duration_ms, error_message, event_type, ip_address, metadata, session_id, status, user_id), no object field with sub-properties, and 0 documents. app-188-index-x has 523 top-level mapped fields (130 boolean, 129 float, 131 long, 132 text, 1 date), of which the vast majority are machine-generated-looking names — counter_0001…counter_0517, flag_0002…flag_0518, label_0003…label_0519, metric_0000…metric_0516 — alongside @timestamp, event_type and user_id; no nested sub-fields exist, so 523 is also its total field count. That is roughly 52x the field count of the sibling indices, and is by far the outlier, but the link to the reported mapping errors and slow indexing is a hypothesis, not a verified fact: the target contains only these four indices (no log index), so no mapper_parsing/error log evidence and no indexing-latency measurement could be read, and the relevant index settings (e.g. index.mapping.total_fields.limit) are not exposed by the mappings tool.

claims.text: Exactly four indices match the pattern app-188-index-*: app-188-index-a, app-188-index-b, app-188-index-c (each health green, docs.count 0, store.size 227b) and app-188-index-x (health green, docs.count 1, store.size 204.4kb).

A cluster-wide index listing on the same target (pattern *) returned only these same four app-188-index-* indices, so no application, error or log index exists in this Elasticsearch target to corroborate mapping errors or indexing latency.

app-188-index-a maps exactly 10 top-level fields: @timestamp, action, duration_ms, error_message, event_type, ip_address, metadata, session_id, status, user_id; no field in its mapping has nested sub-properties.

app-188-index-b maps exactly 10 top-level fields with the same names (@timestamp, action, duration_ms, error_message, event_type, ip_address, metadata, session_id, status, user_id) as app-188-index-a.
app-188-index-c maps exactly 10 top-level fields with the same names as app-188-index-a and app-188-index-b.

app-188-index-x maps 523 top-level fields, far above its three siblings' 10: the mapping contains @timestamp, event_type and user_id plus long runs of generated-style names (counter_0001…counter_0517, flag_0002…flag_0518, label_0003…label_0519, metric_0000…metric_0516).

The 523 mapped fields of app-188-index-x break down by type as 130 boolean, 1 date, 129 float, 131 long and 132 text, and none of them is an object field carrying sub-properties, so 523 is its complete field count rather than a top-level-only count.

app-188-index-a, app-188-index-b and app-188-index-c were checked directly and each shows the same compact 10-field mapping with no nested sub-fields, so the field-bloat pattern seen on app-188-index-x is not shared by those three indices.

The 523-field mapping of app-188-index-x is the likely source of the reported mapping errors and slow indexing on this index family: the generated counter_*/flag_*/label_*/metric_* fields inflate the cluster-state/mapping size and would make any further automatic field addition hit mapping limits or produce rejections. This is unverified because no mapper_parsing/error log, indexing-latency metric or index.mapping.total_fields.limit setting was available in the queried target.

Read app-188-index-x's index settings (index.mapping.total_fields.limit, index.mapping.depth/nested limits) and the Elasticsearch server log for mapper_parsing_exception / Limit of total fields errors to turn the hypothesis into a confirmed cause, then consider replacing the catch-all mapping on event_type-bearing documents with explicit mapping plus a dynamic template that maps unknown counter_*/flag_*/label_*/metric_* fields as disabled or keyword, or reindex into a new index with that stricter mapping.

gaps: No mapping-error or indexing-latency evidence could be read: the registered Elasticsearch target holds only the four app-188-index-* indices (no log/error index), and no Elasticsearch error log or metric source is available in this Run, so the reported 'mapping errors and slow indexing' is neither verified nor quantified.
Index settings such as index.mapping.total_fields.limit are not exposed by elasticsearch_mappings, so whether app-188-index-x's 523 fields exceed or approach its configured field limit is unknown.

The time at which the 523-field mapping on app-188-index-x was created or expanded is unknown: the mappings tool returns only current state, and the change_history integration is not available in this Run.

Whether app-188-index-x is the write target for current event traffic is unknown; it holds 1 document while app-188-index-a/b/c hold 0, and no alias or write-index configuration was readable in this Run.
No Jaeger/Prometheus/Kubernetes check was made for services writing to these indices, so any application-side impact of the field bloat is unchecked rather than shown to be absent.
next_steps: Inspect GET app-188-index-x/_settings and GET app-188-index-x/_alias (outside this read-only Run's tool set) for index.mapping.total_fields.limit, dynamic settings, and whether it is the active write index.
Search the Elasticsearch server logs for 'Limit of total fields', mapper_parsing_exception and 'failed to parse' entries covering the incident window.
Compare index stats (indexing rate, merge/throttle time, indexing failures) for app-188-index-x against app-188-index-a/b/c to quantify the reported slowness.
Review the producer that writes counter_*/flag_*/label_*/metric_* field names — these look programmatically generated and are the probable source of the field inflation.
